newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end up, 30-yr yld hits 1-1/2 yr low.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end up, 30-yr yld hits 1-1/2 yr low.

text.p: Waves of fresh buying boosted U.S. Treasuries early and often, and ended sharply higher on Wednesday, sending the 30-year bond yield to its lowest level in nearly a year and a half.

The 30-year bond closed at its intra-day high of 104-2/32, up 30/32 from Tuesday. Its yield fell to 6.32 percent from 6.38 percent, its lowest since the bond yield closed at 6.25 percent on February 16, 1996.
"Everything is perfect for bonds," said Neil DeSarno, head government bond trader at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp.
Indeed, the long end heavily outpaced the short end on Wednesday, evidenced by the two- to 30-year spread narrowing by three basis points to a 56-basis-point spread.
The rally started during the night in overseas trading, largely on buying during the London session. Buying from just about everywhere extended the gains in the U.S.
Traders reported heavy central bank buying in five-year notes and hedge fund buying in bonds, along with a continuation of convexity flows out of mortgages and into 10-year Treasuries.
Stops at 116-15/32 on the September contract triggerd more buying from so-called day traders, dealers noted.

Adding support to the market was a favorable housing report. While single-family home sales rose 6.1 percent, as expected, to an 819,000 annual unit rate in June, the market cheered a sharp downward revision in May to an annualized 772,000 from the initially reported 825,000 units.
Profit-taking emerged throughout the day, but the ensuing dips were quickly bought.

"Today has been like getting into a fight in a telephone booth; there was nowhere to go," said Brett Benza, senior trader at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp, noting the brisk two-way flows.

Volume was the heaviest of the week at nearly $90 billion, according to GovPX. But after being 25 percent higher than average at midday, volume ended the day only 12 percent higher than average on slow afternoon volume, GovPX noted.

Late in the afternoon, the Treasury announced details of next week's quarterly refunding. As expected, Treasury will sell $16.0 billion three-year notes on Tuesday, $12.0 billion 10-year notes next Wednesday and $10.0 billion 30-year bonds a week from Thursday.
Treasuries moved slightly lower on profit-taking, but headed higher into the close.

Traders said that both fundamental and technical factors should continue to support the bond market. Along with no signs of an acceleration in inflation, a federal budget deal leading to decreased supply and a strengthening dollar were seen pushing the market even higher.
However, Benza said that sellers should emerge once the bond falls to 6.25 percent.

In late trading, the two-year note was at 100-7/32, up 2/32, to yield 5.76 percent. The 10-year note was up 13/26 at 104-6/32 to yield 6.05 percent and the five-year note was at 100-7/32, up 7/32, to yield 5.95 percent.
Bill rates were down two basis points to up one basis point.
